subject: physics_2
question_text: Compare the properties of para, dia and ferromagnetic substances.

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are both STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked: dia — feeble magnetisation opposite to the field, moves strong→weak, χ small negative, μ_r < 1; para — feeble along the field, moves weak→strong, χ small positive, μ_r slightly > 1; ferro — strong along the field, moves strongly weak→strong, χ large positive, μ_r very large; μ_r = 1 + χ links the signs; example sets match the book's table. The book's three-column table is rendered as six property rows, each row comparing the three classes, property name leading.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: How they magnetise

lines.text: Dia: feeble, opposite to the applied field.
Para: feeble, along the applied field.
Ferro: strong, along the applied field.

steps.margin_note: Answer as labelled rows — property first, then Dia / Para / Ferro on their own lines. This row is the defining one.
steps.why: The three classes are defined by their response to the same applied field — with it or against it, feeble or strong. Every later row follows from this one.
common_mistakes: Swapping dia and para. Dia is the class magnetised OPPOSITE to the field.
Writing strongly for para. Para and dia are both feeble; only ferro is strong.

recall.must_convey: That diamagnetic substances magnetise feebly against the field, paramagnetic feebly along it, and ferromagnetic strongly along it.
accept: dia is opposite to the field
para is feebly along the field
ferro is strongly along the field
reject: moves from strong field to weak

steps.memory_tip: Dia = against, para = along but weak, ferro = along and strong.

steps.label: Behaviour in a field
lines: 2. A rod suspended freely in a uniform field:

lines.text: Dia: rests perpendicular to the field.
Para: rests along the field direction.
Ferro: rests along the field direction.
Dia: moves from strong field to weak field.
Para: moves from weak field to strong field.
Ferro: moves strongly from weak to strong.

steps.margin_note: Rows 2 and 3 together are one mark — the rod test and the non-uniform-field test.
steps.why: Both rows restate row 1 as motion: a substance magnetised along the field is pulled toward the stronger field and settles along it; one magnetised against the field is pushed toward the weaker field and settles across it.
common_mistakes: Saying a diamagnetic rod rests along the field. It rests perpendicular — its magnetisation opposes the field.
Saying a diamagnetic material moves to the stronger field. It is repelled, strong to weak.
Forgetting that ferro also moves weak to strong — the same way as para, only strongly.

recall.must_convey: That a diamagnetic rod rests across the field and moves toward the weak field, while para and ferro rest along it and move toward the strong field.
accept: para and ferro move weak to strong

steps.memory_tip: Whatever magnetises along the field goes to the strong region; against the field, to the weak region.

steps.label: χ and μ_r

lines.text: Dia: χ is small and negative.
Para: χ is small and positive.
Ferro: χ is large and positive.
Dia: μ_r is slightly less than 1.
Para: μ_r is slightly greater than 1.
Ferro: μ_r is very large (in thousands).

steps.margin_note: Rows 4 and 5 together are one mark. μ_r = 1 + χ makes row 5 follow from row 4.
steps.why: χ and μ_r turn row 1 into numbers: magnetised against the field means negative χ and μ_r below 1; along the field means positive χ; strong response means large χ. The link is μ_r = 1 + χ.
common_mistakes: Writing μ_r negative for diamagnetic. Only χ is negative; μ_r = 1 + χ stays positive, just below 1.
Writing χ large for paramagnetic. Para χ is small and positive; large positive χ is the mark of ferro.

recall.must_convey: That χ is small negative for dia, small positive for para, large positive for ferro, and μ_r = 1 + χ sits below 1, just above 1, and far above 1 in the same order.
accept: mu r much greater than one for ferro
mu r is one plus chi

steps.memory_tip: μ_r = 1 + χ: put each χ into it and row 5 writes itself.

steps.label: Examples
steps.margin_note: Named substances, one row per class — iron, cobalt, nickel must appear under ferro.
steps.why: The examples row is marked on named substances. The ferromagnetic set is the fixed trio iron, cobalt, nickel (with gadolinium); the other two rows need any two correct names each.
common_mistakes: Putting manganese under ferromagnetic — it is paramagnetic.
Putting oxygen under diamagnetic — oxygen is paramagnetic.
Listing steel as a separate example — steel is an iron alloy; the table asks for elements.

recall.must_convey: That copper and bismuth are diamagnetic, aluminium and manganese paramagnetic, and iron, cobalt, nickel ferromagnetic.

steps.memory_tip: Ferro examples are the magnet metals: iron, cobalt, nickel.

insider_note: Six numbered property rows with Dia, Para and Ferro on their own labelled lines read as the book's table on ruled paper — a prose paragraph loses the comparison and the marks with it.
